proposals.name: Voiced utterance with implied situation, not catalog label
proposals.instruction: Score how far the line reads as something a person would actually say out loud in a moment, in their own voice, AND how much that delivery implies a situation around it. 10 = a complete natural utterance carrying speaker stance (direct address, contraction, exclamation, deixis such as that/this/here) that you could imagine transcribed from real speech, with a scene implied behind it. 5 = a fragment that hints at a speaker but is not actually voiced. 0 = a speakerless noun pile, headline tag, or list of ingredients with nobody behind it.
proposals.rationale: The dense-high half is dominated by voiced lines with a scene behind them: R07 (Y'all know Tater), R18 (Y'all watch this), R53 (Tell you what.), R48 (That's my uncledad!), R24 (We won't do Metric!). The card-high half is dominated by speakerless noun piles: R26 (Swimming Hole Tapeworm), R46 (Third tractor dui), R51 (Family reunion Rohypnol), R39 (WalMart special occasion). The bank appears to be grading ingredient quality; the missing property is performance.

proposals.name: Borrowed stock phrase bent, not merely quoted
proposals.instruction: Applies when the line imports a recognizable pre-existing phrase (lyric, hymn, slogan, bumper sticker, catchphrase). Score how much work the import does beyond recognition. 10 = the borrowed phrase is bent, recontextualized, or turned so the old frame says something new in this contest's world. 5 = lightly repurposed but the meaning is unchanged. 0 = reproduced verbatim as a quotation with no alteration and no new angle, or no borrowed phrase is present and none is needed (score 5 in that case and note it).
proposals.rationale: Dense ranks bent imports at the top: R21 (Pass the ammunition, from the hymn, re-aimed at gun culture, dense .926), R52 (Dog: My Copilot, off God is my copilot, dense .924), R11 (Don't stop me now., dense .946), R01 (We Were Always Great, bending the campaign slogan, dense .988). The card instead rewards a flat verbatim quotation with no turn at all: R54 (Tastes great, less filling, card .963 vs dense .233). Recognition and transformation are being scored as one thing by the bank.

proposals.name: Transformation depth beyond a one-token swap
proposals.instruction: For title/name mashups and puns, score how much idea the substitution adds beyond naming its source. 10 = the swapped element carries a genuine second thought, so the line would still be funny to someone who half-recognizes the source. 5 = a clean substitution that produces one modest joke. 0 = a single letter or word is changed and the entire payload is source recognition, with no observation attached.
proposals.rationale: This is the largest card-over-credit cluster in the slice. R02 (Judge Dread, one letter, card .581 vs dense .037), R57 (All the White Moves, one letter, card .615 vs dense .081), R03 (Kill Bill of Rights, card .799 vs dense .029). The card appears to award full marks for a well-formed substitution regardless of whether the substitution means anything.

proposals.name: Joke left unexplained; no parenthetical gloss
proposals.instruction: Score how much the line trusts the reader to complete it. 10 = the mechanism is never named; the reader does the last step. 5 = a small redundancy restates part of the joke. 0 = an appositive, parenthesis, or trailing clause spells out the wordplay or the target so nothing is left for the reader.
proposals.rationale: Cleanest within-slice matched pair: R48 (That's my uncledad!, ungloss, dense .855) versus R55 (Everybody, my bruncle! (brother + uncle), identical portmanteau device plus a gloss, dense .542). The card is indifferent or positive toward glosses: R32 (16 Angry Men (and one woman), card .841 vs dense .113). Explaining the joke costs dense rank and appears to cost the card nothing.

proposals.name: Single clean payload: no links, spare hashtags, or meta
proposals.instruction: Score the item as a delivery vehicle after ignoring the contest hashtag and the single required @midnight mention. 10 = nothing but the joke; the eye goes straight to the payload. 5 = one minor distraction (stray punctuation, doubled spacing). 0 = the line carries a URL, additional unrelated hashtags, self-promotion, or flattery of the show itself, so attention is split away from the joke.
proposals.rationale: The three lowest dense ranks touching this property are all polluted: R50 (automotive lawn art plus a t.co link, dense .010, card .772), R06 (link plus a self-referential I saw myself on @midnight, dense .049, card .664), R29 (two bolted-on promo hashtags #PointsMe #July4thBirthday, dense .042, card .549). The card gave all three mid-to-high marks, suggesting the bank scores the joke substring and never penalizes the packaging.

proposals.name: Lands on first read without puzzle-decoding
proposals.instruction: Score the reading latency to the laugh. 10 = the joke resolves in one pass, at the speed of scrolling. 5 = a brief double-take that pays off. 0 = the reader must hold two source titles in mind, reverse a word order, or reconstruct a hidden phrase before anything is funny; the line reads as a crossword clue.
proposals.rationale: The card's very top ranks go to the most laborious constructions and dense floors them: R28 (Crouching Hairpiece Hidden Agenda, card .985 vs dense .086), R60 (Carbon Emission Impossible 3: Coal Nation, card .998 vs dense .368), R34 (Speed 2: Control Ted Cruz, which requires reassembling cruise control backwards, card .882 vs dense .179), R05 (What Ever Happened to Baby Jane's Healthcare?, card .723 vs dense .132). Construction effort is visibly being scored as quality.

proposals.name: Cadence: scans cleanly when read aloud
proposals.instruction: Read the line aloud once and score its prosody. 10 = tight rhythm, balanced stresses, alliteration or repetition that makes the line feel finished and quotable. 5 = serviceable but unremarkable. 0 = syllable-padded, lopsided, or typographically clumsy so it stumbles in the mouth (awkward spaced colons, filler conjunctions, one element far longer than the others).
proposals.rationale: Dense rewards pure prosody even where content is generic: R31 (Moonshine, Overalls, Pickups, three matched trochees, dense .934 vs card .145), R37 (Guns, God, Government Corruption, alliterative build, dense .689 vs card .091), R27 (Meth, Meth, Meth, dense .838 vs card .110). Card-favored items with the same subject matter but broken meter sit at the dense floor: R10 (Corn syrup and salt, filler conjunction, card .699 vs dense .071), R43 (12 Angry Men : The Contenders, spaced colon, card .949 vs dense .370).

proposals.name: Playful exploitation of the stated word-count constraint
proposals.instruction: For hashtags that stipulate a word count, score how the line treats that budget. 10 = the constraint is made part of the joke, for example hyphen-stacking to smuggle extra concepts into the legal count, or spending the exact budget so every word is load-bearing. 5 = the count is met unremarkably. 0 = the count is overrun or badly undershot with nothing gained, so the line reads as if it ignored the game.
proposals.rationale: R42 (Deep-fried Chocolate-covered Hostess Twinkie, six concepts hyphenated into four legal words, dense .850 vs card .233) and R09 (Father brother in-law, an entire collapsed family tree inside the exact budget, dense .556 vs card .010) are both dense-high and card-floor. Meanwhile the card rewards overruns: R17 (Jar Jar Binks spin-off movie., card .900 vs dense .172). The bank appears to score topical fit without scoring play against the rule.

proposals.name: List whose final item subverts the preceding ones
proposals.instruction: Applies to enumerations. Score the shape of the list. 10 = the first items establish an expected register and the last item breaks it, so the turn arrives exactly at the end. 5 = a coherent list with a mild escalation. 0 = a flat list of equally weighted items with no turn, or a turn placed in the middle where it deflates. Non-list items score 5.
proposals.rationale: R15 (Guns Nascar Beer Oligarchy, three consumer cliches then a political indictment in the last word, dense .750 vs card .248) and R37 (Guns, God, Government Corruption, dense .689 vs card .091) both put the turn last and are card-floored. The card instead credits flat untwisted lists: R10 (Corn syrup and salt, card .699), R26 (Swimming Hole Tapeworm, card .895), R51 (Family reunion Rohypnol, card .990). The bank seems to score the items, not the ordering.

proposals.name: Nerve: live, specific target together with unhedged delivery
proposals.instruction: Score the risk the line takes, not whether you approve of it, and do not deduct here for offensiveness. 10 = the line names a live figure, faction, or taboo and delivers the hit flat, with no cushioning, hedging, or wink. 5 = a real target handled softly, or a bold delivery aimed at nobody in particular. 0 = targetless, or aimed only at an inert stock butt that no one would object to.
proposals.rationale: The card floors precisely the rows that court offense or partisanship while dense ranks them near the top: R01 (We Were Always Great, dense .988 vs card .162), R23 (Proud Republican Tools, dense .873 vs card .152), R40 (dense .846 vs card .054), R41 (Guns, No Abortions, dense .848 vs card .191), R20 (Trump might actually win., dense .750 vs card .248). The bank looks to be running a safety or civility deduction that is doing double duty as a quality deduction.

proposals.name: Authentic insider idiom versus outsider phonetic caricature
proposals.instruction: Score the lexical texture. 10 = the line uses an idiom a member of the depicted group genuinely says, spelled the way it is actually written, so it reads as ventriloquism from inside. 5 = generic register-appropriate diction. 0 = apostrophes and respellings piled on to signal contempt from outside, producing something no one says and that is hard to read.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high items are real idioms rendered plainly: R35 (Up the Holler, dense .961 vs card .453), R53 (Tell you what., dense .740 vs card .206), R07 (Y'all know Tater, dense .650 vs card .132). The card rewards manufactured eye-dialect that does not resolve: R44 (Readin's For Richies, card .792 vs dense .267), and rewards a plain error as if it were dialect in R33 (Forth grade thirteen-year-old, card .782 vs dense .257).

proposals.name: Deadpan literal answer whose flatness is the indictment
proposals.instruction: Score how well the line works as an anti-joke. 10 = it answers the prompt with a plain, non-joking, literally true statement, and the flatness itself is the punch because of what it implies. 5 = a straight answer with some wit added. 0 = the line strains visibly for a gag, or is flat with nothing implied underneath.
proposals.rationale: A whole dense-high cluster has no detectable joke device at all and must be scoring on implication: R30 (The 4th of July, dense .713 vs card .218), R25 (Need To Get Out, dense .897 vs card .262), R38 (But we're we really?, dense .956 vs card .100), R49 (How Free Are You?, dense .958 vs card .301). A bank of joke-craft criteria would necessarily score these near zero, which is exactly what happened.

proposals.name: Line dies without the contest frame around it
proposals.instruction: Mentally delete the hashtag and re-read the line. 10 = it becomes inert, ordinary, or meaningless on its own, meaning the hashtag is doing indispensable work and the entry is genuinely an answer to this prompt. 5 = it is somewhat funnier with the frame. 0 = it is a self-contained imported gag, a piece of pop trivia, or show-meta that would read identically under any prompt.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high entries are parasitic on their frame in the good way: R21 (Pass the ammunition is nothing without #RedneckIn3Words, dense .926), R52 (Dog: My Copilot, dense .924), R30 (The 4th of July, dense .713). Card-high entries are portable and prompt-agnostic: R54 (Tastes great, less filling is a beer ad wherever you put it, card .963 vs dense .233), R17 (Jar Jar Binks spin-off movie., card .900 vs dense .172), R06 (show-meta plus link, card .664 vs dense .049).

proposals.name: Parses as fluent speech regardless of spelling accuracy
proposals.instruction: Score intelligibility as spoken language, deliberately separating it from orthography. 10 = the line parses instantly as fluent speech on first read even if a word is misspelled, because the error is invisible when heard. 5 = one small stumble. 0 = word order, agreement, or reference is broken badly enough that the reader has to reconstruct what was meant before judging it.
proposals.rationale: Spelling is not what dense is tracking: R38 contains a plain typo (But we're we really?) and still sits at dense .956 while the card floors it at .100, because the typo vanishes when spoken. Conversely the card rewards items whose syntax is genuinely broken: R19 (Me sleeping picture, live alone, card .853 vs dense .326) and R33 (card .782 vs dense .257). A mechanics-and-grammar criterion in the bank would produce exactly this inversion, since it penalizes the harmless case and cannot see the harmful one.

proposals.name: Freshness of angle within the obvious answer space
proposals.instruction: Estimate how many other contestants would have submitted essentially this line. 10 = an angle almost nobody else in a large field would land on. 5 = plausible but findable. 0 = the single most obvious association for this hashtag, the answer a person produces in under two seconds.
proposals.rationale: The card pays full price for the most predictable available move: R03 (Kill Bill of Rights, the first mashup anyone writes for #GOPMovies, card .799 vs dense .029), R02 (Judge Dread, card .581 vs dense .037), R58 (Frenching your sister, the default incest beat, card .740 vs dense .225). Dense reserves its top ranks for angles that are not the first association: R24 (We won't do Metric!, dense .993 vs card .449), R52 (Dog: My Copilot, dense .924 vs card .370). Obviousness appears to be unpriced in the bank.

proposals.name: Handle-first versus payload-first element ordering
proposals.instruction: Report only WHERE the @midnight handle sits relative to the joke text. 10 = the tweet opens with @midnight (or with the contest hashtag) before any joke text, in the shape a reply composed against the show account takes. 5 = the handle sits in the middle, between fragments of payload. 0 = the joke text comes first and the handle is trailing metadata at the end. Count characters and position only. Do NOT judge whether either arrangement is better, more professional, or funnier; you are recording layout, nothing else.
proposals.rationale: This is the single most nearly deterministic surface split in the slice and it has nothing to do with joke quality. Handle-first items are almost uniformly dense_low_card_high: R03, R06, R08, R09, R10, R13, R16, R17, R23, R27, R30, R31, R34, R35, R39, R40, R49. Payload-first items are almost uniformly dense_high_card_low: R15, R21, R24, R41, R45, R50, R52, R54. Two identical-quality jokes typed in the two orders would land in opposite halves of this slice, which is exactly what a nuisance channel looks like.
proposals.upstream_parent: compose method: whether the entry was typed as a reply threaded off the show's account versus composed as a fresh standalone tweet

proposals.name: Internal whitespace irregularity around tags and punctuation
proposals.instruction: Count only anomalous spacing inside the tweet. 10 = multiple doubled spaces separating payload from tags, or a space inserted before a colon or other punctuation that normally has none. 5 = exactly one doubled space anywhere. 0 = single spaces throughout, no space before punctuation. Score the literal character stream. Do NOT treat sloppy spacing as evidence of carelessness or clean spacing as evidence of care, and do NOT judge whether the spacing is good.
proposals.rationale: Doubled spacing before a trailing tag occurs in R02, R14, R15, R21, R22, R25, R26, R45, R50 and R55, every one of them dense_high_card_low; doubled spacing after a leading tag occurs in R10, R31 and R32, every one of them dense_low_card_high; R44 carries a spaced colon (12 Angry Men : The Contenders) and sits at card .949. Whitespace cannot plausibly be a component of how funny an entry is, so any predictive power here is leakage from typing habit, and it is partly collinear with B01.
proposals.upstream_parent: the author's compose client and keyboard habit (mobile app padding, copy-paste of the tag, hand-typed double taps)

proposals.name: Contest hashtag casing fidelity to the canonical form
proposals.instruction: Compare the hashtag as written in the tweet against the canonical CamelCase form given in the CONTEST HASHTAG header. 10 = the casing deviates (all-lowercase, ALL-CAPS, or a partial-case hybrid). 5 = casing matches but spacing or placement of the tag is unusual. 0 = the tag is reproduced in exactly the canonical casing. Report the deviation only. Do NOT judge whether deviant casing looks careless or whether canonical casing looks polished.
proposals.rationale: All three casing deviants in the slice fall on the same side: R40 (#GOPmovies, dense .113 / card .841), R44 (#GOPMOVIES, dense .370 / card .949), R59 (#gopmovies, dense .368 / card .998). The casing of a hashtag is not a property of the joke, but it plausibly indexes how routinely the author plays this game, which could independently affect real entry quality, so this is tagged mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: the author's practice in this nightly format: whether the tag was autocompleted or copied from the show's own post versus retyped from memory

proposals.name: Title-Case styling of the payload as a headline
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the joke text is capitalised in title or headline style. 10 = essentially every content word begins with a capital, as if the entry were the title of something. 5 = mixed, with some words capitalised and some not, or sentence case with one emphatic capital. 0 = entirely lowercase or plain sentence case. Ignore the hashtag and handle when scoring. Do NOT judge whether capitalisation makes the entry look more or less witty, deliberate, or well-crafted.
proposals.rationale: Heavy title casing concentrates in the dense_high_card_low half: R38 (How Free Are You?), R41 (We Were Always Great), R45 (Moonshine, Overalls, Pickups), R47 (Proud Republican Tools), R54 (Need To Get Out), R56 (ACTUAL Sister Wives). All-lowercase payloads concentrate in the other half: R08 (Third tractor dui), R17 (automotive lawn art), R30 (what's a dentist). Capital letters are not humour, but title casing is genre-appropriate in a movie-parody prompt, so it can be entangled with real quality and is tagged mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: the author's formatting habit of presenting an entry as a titled object rather than as typed speech

proposals.name: Payload length and verbosity beyond the prompt's budget
proposals.instruction: Count the joke text only, excluding the handle and the contest hashtag. 10 = long and clause-heavy, roughly forty characters or more, or clearly more words than the prompt's stated budget where one is stated. 5 = moderate, around twenty to forty characters. 0 = very terse, roughly fifteen characters or fewer. Report length as measured. Do NOT reward brevity as punchiness or length as ambition; this is a ruler, not a verdict.
proposals.rationale: The card's very top ranks are occupied by the longest payloads in the slice while dense floors them: R32 (What Ever Happened to Baby Jane's Healthcare?, card .723 / dense .132), R35 (Crouching Hairpiece Hidden Agenda, card .985 / dense .086), R59 (Carbon Emission Impossible 3: Coal Nation, card .998 / dense .368). The shortest payloads run the other way: R15 (Up the Holler, dense .961 / card .453), R20 (Tell you what., dense .740 / card .206), R52 (Meth, Meth, Meth, dense .838 / card .110). A rubric with several craft criteria mechanically has more surface to award on a longer string, so length can inflate a scorecard without any change in how funny the entry is. Tagged mixed because a longer line can also carry a genuinely richer joke.

proposals.name: Bare shortened link indicating an unseen attached image
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the tweet points at content you cannot see. 10 = a t.co or other shortened URL is present and the remaining text does not itself complete a joke, so the payload evidently lives in an attached photo or linked page. 5 = a URL is present but the text stands on its own. 0 = no URL at all. Report only the presence of the pointer and how much of the payload appears to be missing from the text. Do NOT infer that the missing content is either funny or unfunny, and do NOT judge whether linking is good practice.
proposals.rationale: The two link-bearing rows are at or near the dense floor while the card still scores them mid-to-high: R17 (automotive lawn art plus a t.co link, dense .010, the lowest in the slice, card .772) and R11 (a quoted line plus a t.co link, dense .049, card .664). A text-only model necessarily sees a truncated entry here, so the channel predicts a scoring artefact rather than entry quality. Tagged mixed because the unseen photo could genuinely be the best part of the entry.
proposals.upstream_parent: an attached image or media object that carries part or all of the entry and is invisible to any text-only reader

proposals.name: Off-contest metadata load: promo tags, self-reference, show flattery
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the tweet is doing work other than answering the prompt. 10 = additional hashtags unrelated to the contest, self-branding, or text whose subject is the author's own relationship to the show rather than the prompt. 5 = one small off-prompt element. 0 = nothing but the answer plus the required tag and handle. Count the off-prompt material. Do NOT judge whether self-promotion is tacky or whether a clean entry is admirable.
proposals.rationale: R19 carries two bolted-on promotional tags (#PointsMe #July4thBirthday) and sits at dense .042 while the card gave it .549; R11 is entirely about the author having appeared on the show (I saw myself on @midnight) rather than about the prompt, at dense .049 versus card .664. Whether an author is farming attention is a property of the account, not of the joke, so it must not be allowed to enter the bank in either direction.
proposals.upstream_parent: the author's engagement-farming practice: growing reach or courting the show's attention alongside entering the contest

proposals.name: First-obvious-reading versus late-arriving riff on the prompt
proposals.instruction: MODE 3 position fingerprint. Score how much the text reads as written by someone who had already seen many other entries. 10 = it presupposes the obvious answers are taken: a compounded or second-order construction, a deep-cut reference, or a swerve that only makes sense against a field of simpler entries. 5 = a middling angle. 0 = the single most immediate association with the prompt, the answer someone would type within seconds of the hashtag appearing. You cannot see the actual submission order and must not guess it as a number; score only how early-or-late-in-the-stream the writing FEELS. Do NOT judge whether obvious or late answers are better.
proposals.rationale: The slice contains both extremes and they sit at opposite dense ranks despite similar card treatment. First-obvious readings: R09 (Judge Dread, dense .037 / card .581) and R10 (Kill Bill of Rights, dense .029 / card .799). Heavily compounded late-riff constructions: R59 (Carbon Emission Impossible 3: Coal Nation, dense .368 / card .998) and R35 (Crouching Hairpiece Hidden Agenda, dense .086 / card .985). Arrival position is a property of when a person happened to be at their phone, not of the joke, but a later entrant genuinely has more information to work against, so this is tagged mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream and submission timing relative to the rest of the container

proposals.name: Pre-existing title borrowing, a fingerprint of which contest night
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the text is lifted from an already-existing proper title, franchise, slogan, or brand line. 10 = the entry is structurally a pre-existing title with one or more elements swapped. 5 = a named brand, franchise, or public figure appears but the sentence is the author's own. 0 = no borrowed proper title or brand at all. Report the borrowing, not its cleverness. Do NOT judge whether the reference is apt, dated, or well chosen.
proposals.rationale: Container identity is nearly perfectly confounded with the disagreement axis here. Eleven of the thirteen #GOPMovies rows are dense_low_card_high (R06, R09, R10, R13, R23, R29, R32, R35, R40, R44, R59) and all six #ScaryStoryIn5Words rows are dense_low_card_high (R04, R11, R34, R36, R37, R58), while #AmericaIn4Words rows are overwhelmingly dense_high_card_low (R21, R24, R26, R38, R41, R51, R53, R54). Title-borrowing is the visible fingerprint of the borrowing-mandatory prompts, so a bank criterion phrased around reference craft would silently be scoring which night an entry came from.
proposals.upstream_parent: container identity: which night's prompt the item belongs to, since some prompts (movie-title prompts) mandate borrowing and others (identity or word-count prompts) do not

proposals.name: Taboo load: slur, sexual, bodily, or drug content
proposals.instruction: Score how much material is present that a cautious reader would flag. 10 = a slur, an explicit sexual or bodily image, or drugging content stated plainly. 5 = an edgy but conventional taboo topic handled without explicit language. 0 = nothing a cautious reader would flag. Report the presence and explicitness of the material only. Do NOT judge whether the transgression is justified, funny, cruel, or offensive; you are measuring flaggable content, not endorsing or condemning it.
proposals.rationale: The card's floor is occupied by the most flaggable rows while dense ranks them high: R25 (a slur, card .054 / dense .846), R47 (Proud Republican Tools, card .152 / dense .873), R18 (Guns, No Abortions, card .191 / dense .848). At the same time some taboo rows are card-favoured (R34 Great grandmas moist moose knuckle at card .824, R49 Family reunion Rohypnol at card .990), so the channel is not monotone with either model and is clearly tracking an annotation-side reflex rather than entry quality. Tagged mixed because how much offence an entry courts does genuinely affect how a comedy audience receives it.
proposals.upstream_parent: reception-side sensibilities of whoever screens or rates the entries, which apply a safety deduction independent of comedic merit

proposals.name: Inferential compression required to complete the joke
proposals.instruction: Score how much interpretive work the reader must do to complete the joke's underlying logic from a compressed clue, versus having the mechanism spelled out. A 10: the line gives only a compressed clue (a role paradox, a portmanteau, an oblique juxtaposition) and the reader must actively reconstruct the scenario to get the payoff. A 0: the joke's mechanism and target are stated explicitly and literally, leaving nothing for the reader to infer.
proposals.rationale: R28 'Father brother in-law' forces the reader to work out the intermarriage logic themselves and is dense_high_card_low; R51 'That's my uncledad!' similarly withholds the explanation. Contrast R04 'Frenching your sister,' which states the taboo action directly and is dense_low_card_high -- the scorecard rewards the explicit version, the dense model rewards the compressed one.

proposals.name: Avoidance of the single most generic stereotype answer
proposals.instruction: Score how far the entry departs from the single most obvious, first-thing-that-comes-to-mind stereotype for its hashtag category. A 10: an unusual, unexpected angle on the topic that would not be most entrants' default answer. A 0: the most generic, textbook-cliche answer for the category, the kind many entrants would independently submit.
proposals.rationale: R32 'Corn syrup and salt' and R48 'what's a dentist' are both maximally generic, well-worn category answers (junk-food America, toothless-redneck), yet both are card_pct-high while dense_pct is near the floor (0.071, 0.191) -- the scorecard appears to credit safe on-topic genericness that the dense model discounts.

proposals.name: Engagement with the specific prompt vs. format-generic meta-joke
proposals.instruction: Score how tightly the joke's content is bound to THIS specific hashtag prompt, versus being a generic joke about the contest format/act of tweeting itself that could be copy-pasted under almost any other hashtag with no loss of meaning. A 10: the joke could only make sense for this exact prompt/category. A 0: the joke is about tweeting/the account/the show itself and barely engages the prompt's actual topic.
proposals.rationale: R46 'Tweeted from the wrong account #ScaryStoryIn5Words' never tells a scary story at all, and R41 tacks on off-topic hashtags (#PointsMe #July4thBirthday) diluting engagement with #AmericaIn4Words; both are dense_low_card_high, suggesting the scorecard doesn't penalize this format-generic deflection the way the dense model does.

proposals.name: List/enumeration structure with a pattern-breaking final item
proposals.instruction: Score the presence and effectiveness of a short list (2+ items) where the final item breaks the pattern set by the earlier items, producing a twist. A 10: a clean list whose last item clearly subverts or undercuts the expectation set by the prior items. A 0: no list structure, or a list whose items are flat, interchangeable restatements with no capstone twist.
proposals.rationale: R39 'Guns, God, Government Corruption' sets up a patriotic G-alliteration then ends on a corrupt note, and R54 'Guns Nascar Beer Oligarchy' ends on an incongruous political-economic term after three stereotype nouns; both are dense_high_card_low, indicating this twist-list device registers for the dense model but not the scorecard.

proposals.name: Unsoftened commitment to a taboo or bluntly partisan premise
proposals.instruction: Score how fully the tweet commits to a taboo, offensive, or bluntly partisan premise without hedging, softening, or self-censoring the punchline. A 10: the line states its edgy/partisan content plainly, no qualification. A 0: the tweet stays safe/inoffensive or backs away from a stance it gestures toward.
proposals.rationale: R14 'Democrats America's Retarded People' shows the single largest card_pct/dense_pct gap in the slice (dense 0.846 vs card 0.054), and R28 'Father brother in-law' (dense 0.556 vs card 0.010) likewise commits fully to a taboo premise with no softening; the scorecard appears to penalize this bluntness sharply while the dense model does not.

proposals.name: Commitment to a specific character's dialect/persona voice
proposals.instruction: Score how strongly the tweet is written in a specific character's authentic spoken voice (dialect spelling, regional idiom, catchphrase cadence) rather than as neutral third-person description. A 10: distinct dialect/idiom markers place the line unmistakably in a persona's mouth. A 0: neutral, dialect-free phrasing any narrator could have written.
proposals.rationale: R49 'I Speak 'Merican!' and R59 'Tell you what.' both commit to a specific redneck speech register/catchphrase rather than describing a redneck trait from outside; both are dense_high_card_low (0.929/0.409 and 0.740/0.206), suggesting the dense model rewards voice-commitment the scorecard misses.

proposals.name: Brevity-to-punch economy (payoff per word)
proposals.instruction: Score how much comic payoff the line delivers per word, rewarding maximal compression. A 10: very few words (roughly 5 or fewer excluding hashtag/handle), each doing real work, landing a full joke. A 0: the line is padded with words that add apparent construction effort without adding to the payoff.
proposals.rationale: R09 'Meth, Meth, Meth' and R31 'Up the Holler' are both 3-word entries that are dense_high_card_low (0.838/0.110 and 0.961/0.453); contrast the much longer, more elaborately constructed R18 'Carbon Emission Impossible 3: Coal Nation,' which is dense_low_card_high (0.368/0.998) -- the scorecard seems to credit visible construction effort that the dense model does not require.

proposals.name: Original construction vs. single-word-swap into a famous title
proposals.instruction: Score how much original content the line adds beyond a single mechanical word-swap into an already-famous title's exact structure. A 10: built largely from scratch, or the source phrase is altered substantially so most of the comic content is original. A 0: the line just swaps one or two words into an unmistakable famous title while keeping its exact remaining structure, and the swap itself is the entire joke.
proposals.rationale: R01 'Dude, Where Are My Votes?', R10 'The Importance of NOT Being Ernest', and R47 'Judge Dread' are all single-substitution rewrites of famous titles with the rest of the structure untouched; all three are dense_low_card_high, suggesting the scorecard credits this mechanical template move more than the dense model does.

proposals.name: Thematic resonance of a borrowed phrase's original meaning
proposals.instruction: When the tweet borrows a known phrase/lyric/slogan, score how much that phrase's ORIGINAL meaning thematically resonates with the specific hashtag topic, beyond just fitting the required word count. A 10: the borrowed phrase's own subject matter meaningfully echoes or comments on the prompt's theme. A 0: the phrase happens to fit the word count but its original meaning has no thematic connection to the prompt.
proposals.rationale: R55 'Don't stop me now' (Queen, a song about relentless momentum/freedom) plausibly resonates with '#AmericaIn4Words' and is dense_high_card_low (0.946/0.426); contrast R37 'Tastes great, less filling' (a beer-ad slogan with no thematic tie to America beyond word count), which is dense_low_card_high (0.233/0.963).

proposals.name: Full comic payoff realized in text alone, not offloaded to a link
proposals.instruction: Score whether the joke's full comic payoff is realized in the tweet's text alone, versus depending on an external link/image/video a text-only reader cannot access. A 10: the text alone delivers the complete joke with nothing missing. A 0: the tweet includes a link or references unseen media and the text alone is flat or incomplete without it.
proposals.rationale: R24 'automotive lawn art [link]' and R02 '"I saw myself on @midnight" [link]' both attach a URL the reader cannot resolve from text alone, and both sit at the very bottom of the dense_pct distribution (0.010, 0.049) while still card_pct-high, suggesting the scorecard doesn't discount link-dependent payoffs as heavily as the dense model does.

proposals.name: Rhetorical weight that survives a minor surface error
proposals.instruction: Score whether the line carries independent conceptual/emotional weight that survives a minor spelling or grammar slip in the text, versus a slip that leaves nothing else of substance. A 10: even with a visible typo/grammar slip, the line poses a resonant question or observation that lands on its own. A 0: the line has a similar surface slip but is otherwise a flat, low-content statement with no compensating weight.
proposals.rationale: R52 'But we're we really?' has an apparent grammatical slip yet still reads as a weighty rhetorical question about national identity, and is dense_high_card_low (0.956/0.100); contrast R25 'Forth grade thirteen-year-old,' which also has a visible typo ('Forth') but is a flat stereotype statement with no compensating depth, and is dense_low_card_high (0.010/0.772) -- the scorecard seems to penalize surface errors uniformly regardless of the weight they carry.

proposals.name: Familiar-phrase skeleton with one incongruous-register substitution
proposals.instruction: Score whether the tweet takes a familiar fixed phrase/structure from one domain (religious, patriotic, sentimental, wartime) and substitutes one element from a jarringly different-register domain, using the swap to reveal something about a persona. A 10: a clear familiar-phrase skeleton with one element swapped for a jarringly incongruous substitute that recontextualizes the whole phrase. A 0: no recognizable borrowed phrase/structure is being subverted at all.
proposals.rationale: R38 'Dog: My Copilot' recontextualizes 'Jesus is my copilot' by substituting a pet, and R34 'Pass the ammunition' recontextualizes the wartime hymn line 'Praise the Lord and pass the ammunition' into a bare redneck-hashtag context; both are dense_high_card_low (0.924/0.370 and 0.926/0.385), a device the scorecard appears not to credit.

proposals.name: Escalating stacked modifiers building to excess
proposals.instruction: Score whether the tweet stacks multiple escalating descriptive modifiers onto a single noun/image to build up to an absurd or excessive payoff, versus offering a flat, single-note list or description. A 10: two or more escalating modifiers stacked before the payoff noun, each raising the absurdity/excess. A 0: a flat description or bare list with no escalation, every item at the same register.
proposals.rationale: R43 'Deep-fried Chocolate-covered Hostess Twinkie' stacks three escalating modifiers onto one branded object and is dense_high_card_low (0.850/0.233); contrast R32 '#AmericaIn4Words Corn syrup and salt,' a flat two-item list with no escalation, which is dense_low_card_high (0.071/0.699).

proposals.name: Direct rhetorical question implicating the audience
proposals.instruction: Score whether the tweet is phrased as a direct question that implicates or challenges the reader/audience, rather than as a declarative statement or list. A 10: a pointed rhetorical question aimed at the reader that provokes reflection or discomfort. A 0: purely declarative phrasing with no question directed at the audience.
proposals.rationale: R40 'How Free Are You?' and R52 'But we're we really?' are both direct audience-facing questions rather than statements, and both are strongly dense_high_card_low (0.958/0.301 and 0.956/0.100) -- a device the scorecard undervalues relative to declarative entries.

proposals.name: Pun density: multiple independent wordplay hits in one line
proposals.instruction: Score how many independent wordplay hits (distinct puns, homophones, or substitutions) are packed into the single line, each doing its own separate work. A 10: two or more independent wordplay elements stacked in the same short line, each landing its own joke. A 0: at most one simple wordplay element, or none.
proposals.rationale: R08 'Crouching Hairpiece Hidden Agenda' stacks two independent substitutions (Tiger->Hairpiece, Dragon->Agenda) and sits near the very top of card_pct (0.985); R18 'Carbon Emission Impossible 3: Coal Nation' similarly stacks two puns and is card_pct 0.998, near the ceiling of the whole slice -- both far outscore single-substitution entries like R47 'Judge Dread' (card_pct 0.581) within the same dense_low_card_high cluster, suggesting the scorecard rewards pun count in a way the dense model does not track.

proposals.name: Tweet opens with the @midnight mention as first token
proposals.instruction: Score how much the tweet's opening literally begins with the '@midnight' mention/handle before any other content. 0 = @midnight does not appear at the very start of the text; 10 = the text opens with '@midnight' as its first token. This is an extent measure of a formatting/positional convention only -- do NOT judge whether opening with the handle is a good or bad choice.
proposals.rationale: R02 'automotive lawn art', R08 'Swimming Hole Tapeworm', and R09 'Raccoon Defeats Breathalyzer' all open with '@midnight' before the joke content, and all three are dense_low_card_high; this leading-mention convention is plausibly picked up by the scorecard's per-item judge as an unremarkable formatting choice while correlating with something the dense reader discounts, so it should be discounted as a nuisance rather than trusted as evidence of quality either way.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's submission/reply convention (a leading @-mention reads as a Twitter reply, which by default limits the tweet's visibility to mutual followers rather than a full broadcast) or general practice/habit in this format

proposals.name: Hashtag casing deviates from standard camel-case
proposals.instruction: Score how far the hashtag's letter-casing departs from the standard mixed/camel-case convention (e.g. '#GOPMovies'). 0 = hashtag uses standard camel-case with each word capitalized; 10 = hashtag is written in a maximally deviant casing (e.g., fully lowercase, fully uppercase, or otherwise irregular). This is a pure typography extent measure -- do NOT judge whether the casing choice is stylistically good or bad.
proposals.rationale: R03 uses '#gopmovies' (fully lowercase) and R05 uses '#GOPMOVIES' (fully uppercase), both deviating from the standard camel-case form used elsewhere in the slice; both are dense_low_card_high with card_pct near the ceiling (0.998 and 0.949), suggesting this typographic quirk is a candidate nuisance rather than a quality signal.

proposals.name: Numeral+colon franchise-sequel subtitle template
proposals.instruction: Score how much the tweet's title-like phrase follows a numbered-sequel/colon-subtitle pattern typical of real film franchise naming (a numeral after the main title and/or a colon introducing a subtitle). 0 = no such structure present; 10 = the tweet clearly reproduces a numeral + colon-subtitle template mimicking franchise sequel naming. Score only the presence/extent of this structural template, not whether the specific pun content is clever.
proposals.rationale: R03 'Carbon Emission Impossible 3: Coal Nation' and R38 'Speed 2: Control Ted Cruz' both reproduce a numeral+colon franchise-sequel template; both are dense_low_card_high (0.368/0.998 and 0.179/0.882), suggesting the scorecard may reward recognizable adherence to this template independent of the joke's actual originality.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practiced repertoire / frequency of submitting in this exact movie-title-mashup format

proposals.name: Raw count of hashtag tokens in the tweet
proposals.instruction: Score the raw count of distinct hashtag tokens (words beginning with '#') present anywhere in the tweet text, mapped to a 0-10 extent scale (0 = one hashtag or none, 10 = three or more hashtags). Score only the count present in the text -- do NOT judge whether any additional hashtag is relevant, appropriate, or funny.
proposals.rationale: R31 'Twerking Ever Since 2013 #PointsMe #July4thBirthday' stacks three hashtags including two unrelated to the contest topic, versus the single-hashtag baseline in R47 'Overboard Politics #GOPMovies'; hashtag count is a pure text-surface countable that plausibly reflects an off-topic engagement habit rather than the entry's comedic merit.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's participation in an unrelated fan point-scoring / engagement-farming practice around the show (e.g., stacking extra hashtags like '#PointsMe' hoping for additional visibility)

proposals.name: Visible spelling/grammar irregularity in the text
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the tweet text contains a visible spelling, homophone, or grammatical irregularity that a copyeditor would flag (a wrong-word homophone, subject-verb mismatch, missing word, etc.). 0 = no detectable irregularity; 10 = a clear, unambiguous irregularity is present. Score only whether the irregularity is present and how clear-cut it is -- do NOT judge whether the irregularity helps or hurts the line.
proposals.rationale: R20 'Forth grade thirteen-year-old' (homophone 'Forth'/'Fourth') is dense_low_card_high (0.086/0.985), while R26 'But we're we really?' (grammatical anomaly) is dense_high_card_low (0.956/0.100) -- the same surface irregularity predicts opposite directions depending on what else the line is doing, which is exactly why it should be scored and discounted as a nuisance channel rather than read at face value in either direction.
proposals.upstream_parent: editing/proofreading practice or haste at the moment of submission

proposals.name: Content is about the contest/show itself, not the prompt
proposals.instruction: Score how much the tweet's content is about the contest/show/format itself (referencing other entries, the act of tweeting, appearing 'on' the show, or the submission mechanism) rather than about the specific hashtag prompt's topic. 0 = the tweet is entirely about the prompt's actual topic with no reference to the contest/format itself; 10 = the tweet is primarily or entirely about the contest/format/show rather than the prompt topic. Score only this textual orientation -- do NOT judge whether a meta/format-focused joke is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: R43 'Tweeted from the wrong account #ScaryStoryIn5Words' and R56 '"I saw myself on @midnight" #ScaryStoryIn5Words [link]' both engage with the contest/show format itself rather than telling an actual scary story as the prompt asks; both are dense_low_card_high (0.319/0.939 and 0.049/0.664), consistent with a later/veteran-position fingerprint that a scorecard judge scoring topical relevance criteria might not catch, since the joke still nominally carries the hashtag.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream / this author's prior history of participating in or appearing on the show's run (a meta-riff about the format is more likely to be written by someone already steeped in many prior rounds, i.e. later in the contest's overall run, rather than a first-look response to this specific prompt)

proposals.name: Presence of an attached URL/media link
proposals.instruction: Score whether the tweet text includes a URL or link (e.g., 'http://', 'https://', or a 't.co' shortlink) pointing to external media. 0 = no link present; 10 = a link is present. This is a pure presence/extent measure -- do NOT judge whether the linked (unseen) media would be good or funny.
proposals.rationale: R02 'automotive lawn art http://t.co/7KsyHyBtyG' and R56 '"I saw myself on @midnight" ... https://t.co/UYv3f0Atnm' both attach an external link; both are dense_low_card_high with dense_pct near the floor of the whole slice (0.010 and 0.049), suggesting link-dependence is a strong nuisance predictor that a text-only judge cannot actually verify or discount on its merits.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice of submitting multimedia/photo entries or cross-posting from another platform, rather than composing a pure text joke

proposals.name: Raw word count of the joke content
proposals.instruction: Score the raw word count of the tweet's joke content, excluding the '@midnight' mention and hashtag(s), mapped to a 0-10 extent scale (0 = 2 words or fewer, 10 = 8 words or more). Score only the count of words present -- do NOT judge whether the length is appropriate or effective.
proposals.rationale: R55 'Tell you what.' (3 words) and R42 'Meth, Meth, Meth' (3 words) sit at the low end of word count and are both dense_high_card_low, while R31 'Twerking Ever Since 2013 #PointsMe #July4thBirthday' (longer, multi-clause) is dense_low_card_high; raw length is a purely countable surface proxy that plausibly tracks scorer disagreement without itself being a measure of the entry's quality.

proposals.name: Explicit naming of a real political figure or party
proposals.instruction: Score how explicitly the tweet names a specific, real, currently-active political figure (e.g., a named politician) or political party (e.g., 'Democrats', 'Republican'). 0 = no specific named political figure or party is mentioned; 10 = a specific named political figure or party is mentioned explicitly and unambiguously. Score only the presence of the specific name -- do NOT judge whether invoking that name is funny or apt.
proposals.rationale: R36 'Trump might actually win.' and R16 'Democrats America's Retarded People' both name a specific real political figure or party explicitly; both are dense_high_card_low (0.750/0.248 and 0.846/0.054), suggesting named-entity specificity is a text-surface tell that predicts the dense/scorecard split independent of whatever comedic craft is also present in the line.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's degree of political news engagement / topicality of personal interests at submission time

proposals.name: Doubled/extra whitespace between words, tag, or handle
proposals.instruction: Score the extent of extra/doubled whitespace (two or more consecutive space characters) appearing between the tweet's words, hashtag, or handle. 0 = no doubled whitespace anywhere in the text; 10 = multiple instances of doubled whitespace throughout the text. Score only the presence of this typographic/formatting artifact -- do NOT judge whether it affects readability.
proposals.rationale: R05 '12 Angry Men : The Contenders  #GOPMOVIES  @midnight' and R07 '@midnight  #AmericaIn4Words  Tastes great, less filling' both show doubled spaces around the hashtag/handle, likely an artifact of a particular copy/paste or submission-form workflow; both are dense_low_card_high (0.370/0.949 and 0.233/0.963), making this a candidate text-surface tell worth discounting rather than crediting.

proposals.name: Constraint-efficient meaning
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when nearly every word contributes to a layered, coherent idea; give 0 when the wording is filler or an unconnected list.
proposals.rationale: R06, R17, and R51 compress political or cultural meaning into very few words, suggesting value beyond checklistable joke components.

proposals.name: Title transformation
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when a recognizable title is altered into a fresh, coherent comic premise; give 0 when the title is merely copied or the reference is unintelligible.
proposals.rationale: R03, R14, and R49 all transform familiar titles, but their humor depends on how meaning changes rather than on title recognition alone.

proposals.name: Comic specificity
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the entry identifies a precise subject and sharply defined angle; give 0 when it is only a broad slogan, label, or generic statement.
proposals.rationale: R11, R18, and R34 use specific political framing, whereas R31 and R55 are comparatively generic cultural descriptions.

proposals.name: Coherent incongruity
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when seemingly unrelated elements collide into one intelligible comic image or idea; give 0 when they are merely random words.
proposals.rationale: R38, R50, and R57 combine unlikely elements into readable images, indicating a relationship-sensitive property rather than simple keyword presence.

proposals.name: Inventive language play
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when coined wording, a portmanteau, or a controlled lexical twist is immediately parseable and meaningfully funny; give 0 when word formation is absent or confusing.
proposals.rationale: R07, R08, and R41 depend on novel word construction and altered phrasing, which a checklist may treat as ordinary word presence.

proposals.name: Miniature causal scene
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the words imply a compact event with an agent, action, and consequence; give 0 when they provide only a static label or noun list.
proposals.rationale: R13, R27, and R48 suggest small comic narratives, unlike static entries such as R23 or R55.

proposals.name: Absurd escalation
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when an ordinary premise intensifies into an unexpected extreme while remaining understandable; give 0 when there is no turn or escalation beyond the literal statement.
proposals.rationale: R27, R42, and R57 build toward disturbing or absurd endpoints, revealing a progression that simple topicality measures may miss.

proposals.name: Freshness of angle
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when familiar material receives an uncommon perspective or recombination; give 0 when it is a stock stereotype, cliché, or near-verbatim slogan.
proposals.rationale: R01 and R51 repurpose familiar cultural language, while R23 and R31 rely more directly on conventional imagery.

proposals.name: Concrete visuality
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the wording evokes a specific, vivid scene or object that can be pictured immediately; give 0 when it remains abstract or visually indeterminate.
proposals.rationale: R38, R40, and R42 supply unusually concrete images, suggesting that mental pictureability contributes independently of formal joke structure.

proposals.name: Active hashtag alignment
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the wording actively inhabits and transforms the hashtag’s premise; give 0 when the same line could be posted unchanged under almost any hashtag.
proposals.rationale: R09, R22, and R54 use diction that performs a recognizable subculture, while more detachable lines such as R25 provide little prompt-specific framing.

proposals.name: Ironic reversal
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the surface statement sets up an expectation that a second reading sharply undercuts; give 0 when the wording has only one straightforward meaning.
proposals.rationale: R18, R21, and R29 depend on reversals between apparent assertion and implied criticism or contradiction.

proposals.name: Self-contained delivery
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the complete comic premise and payoff are present in the text alone; give 0 when understanding depends on an unavailable link, image, or unstated context.
proposals.rationale: R39 and R40 explicitly depend on linked material, while R46 delivers its premise entirely through the text.

proposals.name: Phrasing precision
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when grammar, spelling, and idiom are clean or deliberately controlled; give 0 when errors or awkward syntax obscure the intended joke.
proposals.rationale: R21, R35, and R45 contain distracting grammatical or spelling irregularities, showing that surface precision can separate fluent comedy from merely recognizable concepts.

proposals.name: Distinctive persona
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when diction creates a specific, memorable speaker or worldview; give 0 when the wording sounds anonymous and interchangeable.
proposals.rationale: R02, R52, and R54 project distinct voices through politically or regionally marked diction rather than through premise alone.

proposals.name: Rhythmic landing
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when cadence, parallelism, or final-word placement makes the line snap and land cleanly; give 0 when the phrasing is flat, clumsy, or rhythmically unresolved.
proposals.rationale: R10, R47, and R50 use compact idiomatic rhythms with strong endings, indicating a delivery-level property not captured by topic or reference counts.

proposals.name: Layout irregularity
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text contains unusual spacing, capitalization, punctuation, or typography; do not judge whether this is good.
proposals.rationale: Formatting residue may correlate with authoring habits or preprocessing while saying nothing intrinsically about contest quality. Examples include R04 and R13.

proposals.name: Leading marker order
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the contest hashtag or @midnight appears before the substantive phrase; do not judge whether this ordering is good.
proposals.rationale: Posting conventions can leave marker-order fingerprints that affect text processing without reflecting the entry itself. Examples include R07 and R10.

proposals.name: Film-title skeleton
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the entry imitates recognizable movie-title syntax, including subtitles, sequels, or title-case phrasing; do not judge the parody's quality.
proposals.rationale: Experienced format participants may reuse familiar title-parody structures, and that practice may also genuinely improve construction. Examples include R03 and R29.

proposals.name: Partisan lexicon
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of explicit partisan, ideological, national, or political vocabulary; do not judge whether the stance is effective.
proposals.rationale: Anticipating an audience can produce overt political vocabulary, while the same targeting may also shape the substantive premise. Examples include R19 and R60.

proposals.name: Named-brand anchoring
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text depends on a named person, product, character, place, or franchise; do not judge whether the reference is apt.
proposals.rationale: Audience-specific familiarity can encourage recognizable names and brands; those references may also genuinely contribute to the joke. Examples include R01 and R05.

proposals.name: Rushed orthography
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of apparent typos, malformed grammar, missing words, or nonstandard spelling; do not judge whether the resulting line is good.
proposals.rationale: Rushed production or limited editing leaves visible language errors, and time pressure can also affect genuine construction quality. Examples include R21 and R59.

proposals.name: Self-explanatory gloss
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the entry adds a parenthetical, qualifier, or explanatory gloss; do not judge whether the explanation helps.
proposals.rationale: Anticipating ambiguity or receiving editing help can leave explicit explanation in the text; clarification may also affect the actual entry. Examples include R17 and R25.

proposals.name: External media residue
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the presence of URLs, quotation artifacts, or wording that visibly points to attached or external media; do not judge whether the material is useful.
proposals.rationale: A sharing or copy-paste workflow can leave media residue that is unrelated to the line's intrinsic quality. Examples include R12 and R38.

proposals.name: Late-riff fingerprint
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the wording reads like a highly specific variation written after obvious prompt interpretations were exhausted; do not judge whether the variation is funny.
proposals.rationale: A late position in a crowded stream may induce narrow mashups or sequel-like variations; that position can also constrain the genuine premise. Examples include R35 and R47.

proposals.name: Borrowed slogan residue
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the entry reuses a familiar advertising slogan, catchphrase, lyric-like phrase, or stock wording; do not judge whether the borrowing works.
proposals.rationale: Exposure to common phrases can create recognizable textual residue, while the same material may also contribute genuinely to the premise. Examples include R13 and R44.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's prior exposure and reuse habits

proposals.name: Unexpected Semantic Collision
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when two unlike concepts collide unexpectedly yet form an immediately intelligible joke; score 0 when the elements remain unrelated or predictable.
proposals.rationale: R08 and R43 turn compact, unrelated concepts into recognizable comic constructions, unlike more literal entries.

proposals.name: Idiomatic Fluency
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the wording sounds natural, polished, and culturally idiomatic; score 0 when grammar, word choice, or phrasing is noticeably malformed.
proposals.rationale: R03 and R30 use fluent vernacular phrasing, while R33 and R52 contain distracting grammatical problems.

proposals.name: Concrete Visualizability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the tweet evokes a vivid, specific scene that can be pictured instantly; score 0 when it remains vague, abstract, or generic.
proposals.rationale: R11 and R57 create sharply visual situations, whereas several high-card entries rely on less concrete wording.

proposals.name: Coinage Craftsmanship
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an invented word or blend is both immediately understandable and elegantly compact; score 0 when no inventive coinage appears or a coinage is confusing.
proposals.rationale: R43’s “uncledad” and R48’s “bruncle” demonstrate compact, decipherable word formation that a checklist may overlook.

proposals.name: Layered Comic Escalation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when successive words add increasingly excessive or surprising detail to the same comic premise; score 0 when the wording is a flat list with no escalation.
proposals.rationale: R17 stacks indulgent modifiers around one object, and R28 builds an increasingly pointed sequence of national symbols and power; R14 is comparatively flat.

proposals.name: Distinctive Speaker Voice
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the wording strongly suggests a specific, consistent comic persona; score 0 when it could have been written by anyone without a discernible voice.
proposals.rationale: R36 and R47 convey a recognizable vernacular speaker, while R44 mostly presents interchangeable stereotype nouns.

proposals.name: Ironic Premise Reversal
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the literal wording turns back on itself to expose a clear comic contradiction; score 0 when the statement is entirely literal and unreversed.
proposals.rationale: R22 uses resistance to the metric system as an ironic national claim, and R41 turns freedom into a pointed question rather than a description.

proposals.name: Satirical Target Precision
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the joke makes its precise social or political target unmistakable; score 0 when it merely strings together topical terms without a discernible point.
proposals.rationale: R18 identifies government corruption within a compact value cluster, and R28 specifies oligarchy; R05 and R37 are more topical than pointed.

proposals.name: Title Transformation Depth
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a recognizable title is transformed into a new phrase with a coherent, specific comic meaning; score 0 when only a superficial word substitution or title echo is present.
proposals.rationale: R21 and R25 retain recognizable title scaffolds but provide relatively weakly developed new premises, revealing the difference between title resemblance and substantive transformation.

proposals.name: Standalone Comprehensibility
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the joke can be understood from the tweet’s wording with little outside context; score 0 when its meaning depends on unexplained lore, references, or missing context.
proposals.rationale: R34 and R57 communicate their situations directly, while R40 and R50 depend heavily on familiarity with specific fictional references.

proposals.name: Constraint-Native Phrasing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the requested word-count format feels deliberately exploited as part of a natural, complete phrase; score 0 when the wording feels truncated, padded, or accidentally shaped by the constraint.
proposals.rationale: R16 and R22 make their four-word form feel intentional and complete, whereas R33 and R52 show strain within the same kind of constraint.

proposals.name: Memorable Cadence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when rhythm, repetition, or sound makes the line especially punchy when read aloud; score 0 when its cadence is inert, clumsy, or forgettable.
proposals.rationale: R45 uses emphatic repetition and R19 has a crisp spoken rhythm, while R21 and R23 are more awkward to say and retain.

proposals.name: Taboo Integration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when provocative or taboo material is integrated into a specific comic mechanism; score 0 when offensiveness or shock is the entire joke.
proposals.rationale: R26 and R54 attach taboo material to distinct premises, allowing judges to separate constructed transgression from merely provocative wording.

proposals.name: Resistance To Stock Shorthand
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the tweet avoids obvious stereotype bundles by finding a fresh angle; score 0 when it relies mainly on familiar cultural shorthand or expected labels.
proposals.rationale: R11 and R57 approach their themes through unusual situations, whereas R44 and R45 depend heavily on stock redneck associations.

proposals.name: Punchline Closure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the final word or phrase delivers a complete, decisive comic payoff; score 0 when the line stops at setup, ambiguity, or an unfinished thought.
proposals.rationale: R12 and R34 culminate in clear final beats, while R03 and R49 feel more like setups lacking a fully closed punchline.

proposals.name: Wrapper orientation
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the entry uses a standardized wrapper with @midnight and the contest hashtag arranged in a conventional order; judge only the arrangement, never whether it is good.
proposals.rationale: Copied submission templates can systematically affect text presentation without expressing comedic merit. Leading wrappers appear in R02, R09, and R24, while trailing wrappers appear in R03, R11, and R18.

proposals.name: External-artifact residue
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text contains a URL, attachment cue, quoted copied wording, or other platform artifact; judge only the artifact's presence, never whether it improves the entry.
proposals.rationale: Links and attachment-like traces may reflect posting mechanics or reuse rather than the entry itself. R02 and R46 contain URLs, while R42 contains an explicit picture-related cue.

proposals.name: Dialect orthography
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the entry uses nonstandard dialect spelling, vernacular contractions, or persona-marking orthography; judge only the amount of such spelling, never whether it is effective.
proposals.rationale: A practiced entrant may repeatedly use recognizable vernacular markers, which can influence reception while also plausibly reflecting genuine writing skill. Examples include R20, R38, R45, and R52.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practiced persona or format experience

proposals.name: Entertainment-reference density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the entry relies on named films, characters, songs, or other entertainment references; judge only reference density and recognizability, never whether the reference is apt.
proposals.rationale: Audience familiarity and learned reference associations can systematically affect processing without being comedic merit. Film or character references appear in R03, R13, R17, R26, R28, and R50.

proposals.name: Ideological signaling
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the entry contains explicit political, partisan, patriotic, governmental, or culture-war language; judge only the amount of signaling, never whether the stance is good.
proposals.rationale: Audience identity and polarization can alter reactions to political wording independently of the entry's construction. Explicit signals occur in R12, R18, R19, R25, and R44.

proposals.name: Commercial-brand cues
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the entry uses consumer products, retailers, advertising slogans, or brand-like commercial language; judge only the amount of commercial cueing, never whether it is humorous.
proposals.rationale: Commercial vocabulary may trigger familiarity or memorability effects unrelated to contest quality. Examples include the slogan in R06, Hostess in R35, and WalMart in R56.

proposals.name: Taboo lexicon
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the entry uses sexual, bodily, drug-related, assault-related, or otherwise taboo vocabulary; judge only lexical presence, never offensiveness or comedic value.
proposals.rationale: Norms and sensitivity around taboo terms can create systematic reactions without describing how well the entry is made. Such vocabulary appears in R10, R19, R30, R58, and R60.

proposals.name: Platform self-reference
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the entry refers to accounts, posting, the show, being seen, personal promotion, or contest participation; judge only the degree of self-reference, never whether it is effective.
proposals.rationale: Platform-oriented authors may leave self-referential traces that attract attention or familiarity independently of the text's comedic construction. Examples include R09, R21, and R46.

proposals.name: Telegraphic list syntax
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the entry is a bare noun list or comma-separated fragment with omitted connective words; judge only syntactic form, never whether the compactness is good.
proposals.rationale: Repeated format practice can produce a stable list-writing fingerprint that affects reception while also plausibly accompanying genuine skill. Clear examples include R12, R43, and R58.

proposals.name: Prompt-first canonicality
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the wording looks like an immediate stock completion of the prompt through a short familiar phrase or title substitution; judge only this textual fingerprint, never whether the riff is good.
proposals.rationale: Early or crowded-stream submissions may leave direct first-association wording, while later submissions may show more layered construction; actual position is unavailable and must not be inferred. Bare title substitutions appear in R26 and R29, while more layered variants appear in R36 and R51.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream or submission timing
